title: NexusAI
tagline: One chat box, eight specialist agents — routed cheaply, grounded in tools, guarded on the way in and out.
summary: A multi-agent assistant where a MasterOrchestrator sends each turn to one or more of eight GPT-4o specialist agents. Each specialist runs a ReAct tool-calling loop over 31 tools, and the answer streams as typed events to a Streamlit UI and to an Android app through a FastAPI/SSE gateway.
problem: People ask about unrelated things in one conversation — weather, news, money, careers — and shouldn't have to pick a mode first. But sending every message through an LLM router adds delay and cost, free public APIs are flaky, and user input can carry prompt injection or personal data.
objective: Route each request to the right specialist cheaply, ground answers in real tool data, fail safely when a source is down, and keep every step observable and testable offline.
approach: Custom Python orchestration engine: a MasterOrchestrator runs a seven-stage pipeline on every turn — input guardrails, routing, clarification, concurrent fan-out, aggregation, output rails and a single-writer memory commit.

Four-stage hybrid router: keyword rules first, then follow-up context, then a GPT-4o JSON classifier, then a fallback. The classifier's output is validated, and a confidence floor turns uncertain turns into a clarifying question instead of a guess.

Each specialist is built by an agent factory from a playbook, a prompt, guardrail overlays and a tool allow-list, and runs a ReAct loop with an iteration cap — the final round runs without tools to force an answer.
Tools are declared with a decorator that generates the function schema from the Python signature. Tools never raise: each returns a structured result with a status, recovery hint and source label.
When several agents run, their outputs merge into one stream through an asyncio queue, and an aggregation step combines the answers.
One typed event format feeds both clients: the Streamlit web app and the Android app over the FastAPI/SSE gateway.

challenges.challenge: Routing every turn through an LLM is slow and costly, but pure rules misroute paraphrases.
challenges.solution: A router that tries the cheapest method first and only escalates when needed, with a confidence margin check and a clarification floor for genuinely ambiguous turns.

challenges.challenge: Free public APIs fail or rate-limit unpredictably.
challenges.solution: Tools never raise. They return structured results and fall back to deterministic sample data, which the agents must disclose to the user.

challenges.challenge: Prompt-injection text could re-enter the model through conversation history.
challenges.solution: Blocked input is stored only as a withheld placeholder, and memory saves only text that has passed the output guardrails.

challenges.challenge: Streamlit reruns synchronously while the engine is fully async.
challenges.solution: The engine runs on a background thread's event loop that is cancelled cleanly on rerun; tracer spans always close, and one failing parallel agent doesn't stop the others.

quality: A fake LLM client lets the whole suite run without spending tokens.
All network calls go through one seam, so a single fixture can cut the network and exercise every tool's fallback path.

title: IntelliHub
tagline: One question in, one sourced briefing out — news, markets, jobs and lab reports, with every figure computed in Python.
summary: A multi-agent intelligence platform. A plain-Python ReAct-style planner decides which domain agents to run, executes them concurrently, and merges their results into one briefing with sources, a status and token cost. Each domain agent wraps a Microsoft AutoGen AssistantAgent that calls its own tools.
problem: The information behind everyday decisions is scattered across news and RSS feeds, research APIs, market data, government job portals and lab-report PDFs. Pulling it together by hand is slow, inconsistent and leaves no record of where each fact came from.
objective: Turn one free-text question into a single sourced briefing that can be tested, stored and demoed at zero API cost.
approach: A deterministic intent classifier scores the query, picks the agents, a strategy (concurrent or sequential), a confidence and a time window — then a planner builds the execution plan.
Collector agents run concurrently with asyncio.gather; the health pipeline runs afterwards, in a fixed order.
Each domain agent wraps an AutoGen AssistantAgent whose tools are AutoGen FunctionTools. Full tool results go to a side collector; the model sees only a short status line.
The LLM writes prose only. Every schema-bearing section is computed in Python, so figures are reproducible and testable.
Six layers talk only through typed Pydantic contracts; agents are built lazily, only when a request needs them.
A deterministic mock implements AutoGen's real client interface — turn one requests every tool, turn two writes the narrative — so the full agent loop runs without API keys.
features: Multi-domain answers from a single question
Honest status: PARTIAL when only some agents succeed, sample data marked DEGRADED when the network fails
Lab-value trends with abnormal-value flags and a risk score
Health access limited to an allowed-user list, with a mandatory medical disclaimer on every path
Streamlit chat, file upload and dashboard; optional ChromaDB memory with an in-memory fallback

challenges.challenge: No API budget for development and demos.
challenges.solution: A deterministic mock that implements AutoGen's real client interface, so the true agent and tool loop runs keyless.

challenges.challenge: LLM output is unstable for anything numeric or structured.
challenges.solution: The model writes prose only; Python computes every structured section, which also makes the briefing testable.

challenges.challenge: Health data needs stronger safety than the other domains.
challenges.solution: An allowed-user check runs before any data is read, a disclaimer is attached on every path, and history is read before saving.

challenges.challenge: A misconfigured deployment could silently fall back to the mock.
challenges.solution: A require-live flag that fails loudly with a configuration error, plus a mock-mode warning and a verify command.

quality: 357 tests across 31 files pass without API keys.

title: RAG-Powered QA for Medical Research
tagline: Ask questions of a library of research PDFs and get grounded answers and summaries.
summary: Automates question answering and summarisation over medical-research PDFs stored in AWS S3. Text is extracted from each PDF, embedded with OpenAI embeddings and indexed in FAISS; user questions retrieve the most relevant passages, which GPT-4 uses to answer.
problem: Researchers lose time searching long PDFs for specific findings, and a general-purpose chatbot answers from memory rather than from the papers in front of them.
objective: Answer questions and summarise papers using only the content of a given document collection.
approach: Load research PDFs from cloud storage (AWS S3) with boto3.
Extract text with PyPDF2 and generate embeddings with the OpenAI API.
Index embeddings in FAISS for fast similarity search.
At question time, retrieve the most relevant passages and pass them to GPT-4 through LangChain to answer or summarise.
Expose question answering and summarisation through a REST API.

title: Autonomous Code Generation & Execution
tagline: Two AutoGen agents — one writes code, one runs it — iterating until the task works.
summary: A multi-agent system built with Microsoft AutoGen that automates code generation and execution. Conversable agents with specialised roles — a Code Writer Agent and a Code Executor Agent — collaborate on a task inside an isolated virtual environment.
problem: LLM-generated code often fails on first run, and a human has to copy, run and report errors back by hand.
objective: Close the loop automatically: generate code, execute it safely, feed results back, and iterate.
approach: Define two conversable AutoGen agents with distinct roles and system messages.
The Code Writer Agent (GPT-4o) proposes code for the user's task.
The Code Executor Agent runs it in an isolated virtual environment and returns output or errors.
The agents iterate until the task succeeds or a turn limit is reached.
